---
title: "Basis and Dimension — The Fewest Directions You Need"
description: "An original mathematical walkthrough with one running example, concrete numbers and a proof."
---

## Ask a simple question

If east and north already let you reach every point on a flat map, do you need a third arrow pointing northeast?

## Build the intuition

A basis contains independent vectors that span the space. Dimension counts how many directions are needed in any basis.

## Write the mathematical relationship

$$
\mathbf x=3\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** x is the vector (3,2); the two column vectors are standard basis directions in ℝ²; coefficients 3 and 2 tell how many units of each direction to combine.

**Substitute real numbers:** Three horizontal steps plus two vertical steps give (3,2). A northeast arrow (1,1) equals the sum of the two basis vectors, so it adds no new independent direction.

## Why the relationship is true

Independence means none of the basis vectors can be formed by combining the others; spanning means every vector can be formed from them. Both properties are necessary.

## Where the shortcut stops working

Coordinates change if the basis changes, but the underlying geometric vector need not change. Do not confuse coordinates with the vector itself.

## Your turn

Does {(1,0),(2,0)} form a basis of ℝ²? Which requirement fails?

**Source structure:** Ivan Savov, *No Bullshit Guide to Linear Algebra*, second edition, Geometric aspects, §§4.4–4.5. This is an independently written explanation based on the uploaded **extended preview**, not a transcription of the commercial full book.
